concept.name: Binary Indexed Tree: Difference Arrays, Range Updates & Binary Lifting
concept.title: Binary Indexed Tree: Difference Arrays, Range Updates & Binary Lifting

spark.summary: Beyond basic point-update prefix sums, Binary Indexed Trees (Fenwick Trees) support O(log N) range-add + range-sum via dual difference arrays and O(log N) k-th order-statistic search via binary lifting in a flat N+1 array.
spark.keyTakeaway: Using lowest-set-bit jumps (idx & -idx), a Fenwick Tree executes <= 20 bit operations for N=1,000,000 and consumes 4x less memory than a 4N Segment Tree.
spark.byteSummary:
A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) stores partial sums over power-of-two ranges of length `idx & -idx` inside a flat, 1-indexed `N+1` array. For `N = 1,000,000`, every point update (`idx += idx & -idx`) and prefix sum (`idx -= idx & -idx`) touches at most 20 cache-friendly array slots—eliminating the 4N node array and pointer/recursion overhead of a Segment Tree.

Two advanced patterns unlock full production versatility without leaving the `N+1` footprint. First, pairing two Fenwick Trees (`BIT1` for `D[i]` and `BIT2` for `i * D[i]`) over a difference array enables both O(log N) range additions and O(log N) range-sum queries.

Second, Binary Lifting walks powers of two (`2^19, 2^18, ..., 1`) top-down over the BIT array in a single O(log N) pass to find the smallest index whose prefix sum reaches `k`—serving real-time P99 quantiles and order-statistic queries without an extra O(log^2 N) binary search.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: Lowest-Set-Bit Responsibility (idx & -idx)
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how two's-complement bit isolation maps each 1-indexed slot to its power-of-two subrange.
learningJourney.explanation: In two's complement, `-idx` flips all bits and adds 1, so `idx & -idx` isolates the lowest set bit (LSB). Slot `BIT[idx]` stores the sum of the `lsb = idx & -idx` elements ending at `idx`: `[idx - lsb + 1 .. idx]`. Because indices must be 1-based (`0` has `0 & 0 == 0` which would loop forever), the array has length `N + 1`.

sectionDiagram.title: Mapping BIT[1..8] to Power-of-Two Subranges via idx & -idx

cards.label: Zero Pointer Chasing
cards.detail: A flat (N+1) array fits in ~8 MB for N=1M (vs 32+ MB for a 4N Segment Tree), boosting L3 cache hits.

cards.label: 1-Based Invariant
cards.detail: Always guard idx >= 1 before entering while loops so idx=0 never stalls.

sectionDiagram.summary: Isolating idx & -idx assigns each 1-based slot a power-of-two subrange inside a compact (N+1) contiguous array.
sectionDiagram.caption: 1-indexed BIT slots cover power-of-two ranges of length idx & -idx inside a flat N+1 array.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: O(log N) Point Update & Prefix Query Loops
learningJourney.purpose: Trace upward parent jumps (idx += idx & -idx) and downward prefix jumps (idx -= idx & -idx).
learningJourney.explanation: To add `delta` at `idx`, we walk upward to every covering ancestor via `idx += idx & -idx` until `idx > N`. To compute `prefix_sum(idx)`, we accumulate `BIT[idx]` and strip the lowest set bit via `idx -= idx & -idx` until `idx == 0`. Both loops execute at most `floor(log2(N)) + 1` iterations (<= 20 ops for N=1M).

sectionDiagram.title: <= 20 Bit Operations per Update or Prefix Sum at N = 1,000,000

cards.label: Invertibility Requirement
cards.detail: Range Sum(L, R) = prefix(R) - prefix(L-1) requires an invertible operator (+/XOR); use Segment Trees for min/max.

cards.label: O(N) Linear Build
cards.detail: Building a BIT from an initial array takes O(N) by propagating tree[i] directly to tree[i + (i & -i)].

sectionDiagram.summary: Upward += lsb updates and downward -= lsb prefix queries run iteratively in <= 20 bit ops for N=1,000,000.
sectionDiagram.caption: Iterative += lsb updates and -= lsb prefix queries complete in <= 20 operations for N=1,000,000.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: O(N) Linear-Time Construction
learningJourney.purpose: Initialize a Fenwick Tree from an existing N-element array in O(N) instead of O(N log N).
learningJourney.explanation: Calling `add(i, arr[i])` N times takes O(N log N). Instead, copy `arr` into `tree[1..N]` and in a single linear pass `i = 1..N`, add `tree[i]` directly to its immediate parent `j = i + (i & -i)` if `j <= N`. Each element is touched once, cutting initialization time by ~10x at N=1M.

sectionDiagram.title: Single-Pass Parent Propagation in O(N) Time

cards.label: Cache-Sequential
cards.detail: Linear sweep over tree[1..N] is hardware-prefetcher friendly.

cards.label: Exact Equivalence
cards.detail: Every slot receives the exact sum of its direct and transitive children in topological order.

sectionDiagram.summary: Propagating each slot to its immediate parent i + (i & -i) builds the Fenwick Tree in O(N) time.
sectionDiagram.caption: Single-pass parent propagation tree[i + (i & -i)] += tree[i] builds a Fenwick Tree in O(N) time.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Range Update + Point Query via Difference Array
learningJourney.purpose: Support O(log N) range additions [L, R] += delta with O(log N) point reads using a single BIT.
learningJourney.explanation: If a workload needs range additions `[L, R] += val` and single-point queries `get(i)`, store the difference array `D[i] = A[i] - A[i-1]` inside a single Fenwick Tree. Range add `[L, R] += val` becomes two point updates: `add(L, +val)` and `add(R + 1, -val)`, while `get(i)` is simply `prefix_sum(i)`.

sectionDiagram.title: Two-Point Range Add & Prefix Point Read in 1 Fenwick Tree

cards.label: Zero Lazy Propagation
cards.detail: Unlike Segment Trees, difference-array BIT needs zero lazy-tag pushdown logic.

cards.label: 2x Updates Per Range
cards.detail: Each range update touches at most 40 array elements for N=1M.

sectionDiagram.summary: Storing a difference array in one Fenwick Tree turns range additions into two point updates and point reads into prefix sums.
sectionDiagram.caption: A single difference-array BIT performs O(log N) range additions via add(L, +v) and add(R+1, -v).

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Dual-BIT for Both Range Updates & Range Sums
learningJourney.purpose: Achieve O(log N) range-add AND O(log N) range-sum using two coupled Fenwick Trees.
learningJourney.explanation: From `sum(1..r) A[i] = sum_{i=1..r} sum_{j=1..i} D[j]`, rearranging the double sum yields `(r + 1) * sum(D[1..r]) - sum(i * D[i] for i in 1..r)` (or `r * sum(D[1..r]) - sum((i-1) * D[i])`). Maintaining `BIT1` for `D[i]` and `BIT2` for `(i-1)*D[i]` gives full O(log N) range-add and range-sum in 2N+2 integers.

sectionDiagram.title: Coupled BIT1(D[i]) + BIT2((i-1)*D[i]) for Range Add & Range Sum

cards.label: 2x Smaller Than SegTree
cards.detail: Dual BIT uses 2N ints vs 4N (or 8N with lazy tags) for a Segment Tree.

cards.label: 64-Bit Overflow Guard
cards.detail: Because BIT2 stores i * D[i], always use 64-bit integers (int64) when N * val > 2^31.

sectionDiagram.summary: Coupling BIT1(D[i]) and BIT2((i-1)*D[i]) supports both O(log N) range updates and O(log N) range sums in 2N+2 ints.
sectionDiagram.caption: Dual Fenwick Trees compute sum(1..r) = r * Query1(r) - Query2(r) for O(log N) range updates and sums.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: O(log N) Binary Lifting for k-th Order Statistics
learningJourney.purpose: Find the k-th smallest element or P99 quantile bucket in a single O(log N) pass without binary search.
learningJourney.explanation: A naive `binary_search + prefix_sum` takes `O(log^2 N)` (~400 ops at N=1M). Binary Lifting exploits the power-of-two structure of `BIT`: iterating `bit = 2^floor(log2(N))` down to `1`, if `pos + bit <= N` and `acc + BIT[pos + bit] < k`, we advance `pos += bit` and `acc += BIT[pos]` in one O(log N) pass (~20 ops).

sectionDiagram.title: Single-Pass O(log N) Quantile & Order-Statistic Search

cards.label: 20x Faster Than Binary Search
cards.detail: Binary lifting drops P99 quantile lookup from O(log^2 N) (~400 ops) to O(log N) (<= 20 ops).

cards.label: Non-Negative Frequencies
cards.detail: Binary lifting requires all underlying frequencies >= 0 so prefix sums are monotonic.

sectionDiagram.summary: Binary lifting walks powers of two top-down over BIT[] to locate the k-th order statistic or quantile in a single O(log N) pass.
sectionDiagram.caption: Binary lifting tests descending powers of two over BIT[] to locate k-th order statistics in <= 20 operations.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Coordinate Compression & 2D Fenwick Extensions
learningJourney.purpose: Handle sparse 64-bit prices/timestamps and 2D spatial grids cleanly within bounded memory.
learningJourney.explanation: When keys span 64-bit integers (like nanosecond latencies or arbitrary stock prices), Coordinate Compression sorts unique keys offline and maps each key to `1..U` via `bisect_left` before indexing into the BIT. For 2D grids (`R x C`), nesting a BIT of BITs computes rectangle sums in `O(log R * log C)`.

sectionDiagram.title: Mapping Sparse 64-Bit Keys to Dense 1..U BIT Indices

cards.label: Fixed-Bucket Alternative
cards.detail: For streaming telemetry where keys aren't known upfront, use log-linear HDR histogram buckets.

cards.label: 2D BIT Trade-off
cards.detail: A 2D BIT takes O(R * C) space and O(log R * log C) time—great for dense grids up to ~4096x4096.

sectionDiagram.summary: Coordinate compression maps sparse 64-bit domains into dense 1..U indices for compact O(log U) Fenwick Tree operations.
sectionDiagram.caption: Coordinate compression maps sparse 64-bit keys via bisect_left() + 1 into a dense 1..U Fenwick Tree.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a Fenwick Tree always use 1-based indexing (`1..N`) rather than 0-based indexing?

options.text: Because `0 & -0 == 0`, so `idx += idx & -idx` and `idx -= idx & -idx` at index 0 would loop infinitely.
options.feedback: Correct. Index 0 has no set bits, so isolating the lowest set bit returns 0 and never advances.

options.text: Because Python and C++ arrays do not allow index 0.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Arrays are 0-indexed, so we allocate size N+1 and leave slot 0 unused.

options.text: Because 0-based indexing requires 4N memory like a Segment Tree.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Memory is N+1 regardless; 1-based indexing is required for bit termination.

options.text: Because `idx & -idx` returns negative numbers for index 0.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Since 0 & -0 is 0, Fenwick Trees leave index 0 unused and operate on 1..N so bit-isolation loops always terminate.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does a Dual-BIT achieve BOTH O(log N) range additions and O(log N) range sums?

options.text: It maintains `BIT1` for the difference array `D[i]` and `BIT2` for `(i-1)*D[i]`, computing `prefix_sum(r) = r * Query1(r) - Query2(r)`.
options.feedback: Correct. Expanding the double sum of the difference array yields that exact linear combination in 2N+2 space.

options.text: It runs a Segment Tree inside `BIT2`.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both structures are flat N+1 Fenwick Trees.

options.text: It rebuilds the prefix-sum array in O(N) after each range add.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rebuilding takes O(N), not O(log N).

options.text: It uses binary lifting on every range addition.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Binary lifting is for k-th order-statistic queries.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Coupling BIT1(D[i]) and BIT2((i-1)*D[i]) evaluates prefix sums of a difference-array-updated sequence in O(log N).

knowledgeChecks.question: What precondition is required for O(log N) Binary Lifting on a Fenwick Tree to return the correct k-th order statistic?

options.text: All underlying element frequencies must be non-negative (>= 0) so prefix sums are monotonically non-decreasing.
options.feedback: Correct. If negative values exist, prefix sums are non-monotonic and greedy power-of-two jumps can miss the true index.

options.text: N must be an exact power of 2.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Checking `nxt <= n` handles arbitrary N safely.

options.text: The BIT must be initialized in O(N log N).
options.feedback: Incorrect. O(N) initialization produces the exact same tree.

options.text: Only point queries (no updates) are allowed.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Binary lifting works dynamically alongside O(log N) updates.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Binary lifting relies on monotonic prefix sums, which hold whenever all frequency counts in the BIT are >= 0.

beginner.summary: A Fenwick Tree stores clever partial sums in a flat array so you can update a bucket or ask for any range sum in ~20 steps even with 1,000,000 buckets.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Using `idx & -idx` bit jumps gives O(log N) updates and range sums using 4x less memory than a Segment Tree.
beginner.byteSummary:
If you have 1,000,000 buckets and update one value, rebuilding a normal prefix-sum array touches all 1,000,000 elements. A Fenwick Tree groups buckets by powers of two using `idx & -idx`.

Each update or range sum only visits up to 20 array slots, keeping both memory and latency tiny.

intermediate.summary: Master O(N) linear construction, single-BIT difference-array range updates, and dual-BIT range-add + range-sum in 2N+2 integers.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Pairing `BIT1(D[i])` and `BIT2((i-1)*D[i])` unlocks full O(log N) range updates and sums without Segment Tree lazy propagation.
intermediate.byteSummary:
Fenwick Trees initialize in O(N) via parent propagation `tree[i + (i & -i)] += tree[i]`. Storing a difference array supports O(log N) range adds with O(log N) point reads.

Adding a second BIT for `(i-1)*D[i]` enables both O(log N) range adds and range sums in half the memory of a 4N Segment Tree.

advanced.summary: Use single-pass O(log N) binary lifting for real-time P99 quantiles and coordinate compression (`bisect_left + 1`) for sparse 64-bit domains.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Binary lifting drops k-th order-statistic queries from O(log^2 N) (~400 ops) to O(log N) (<= 20 ops) on non-negative frequency tables.
advanced.byteSummary:
Binary lifting walks descending powers of two (`2^19 .. 1`) over `BIT[]` to find the k-th order statistic or P99 latency bucket in <= 20 iterations—20x faster than binary-searching prefix sums.

For sparse 64-bit price or timestamp keys, coordinate compression via `bisect_left() + 1` maps keys into a dense `1..U` Fenwick array.

_recommendedProblem.prompt: Replace an O(N) prefix-sum rebuild bottleneck at N=1,000,000 buckets with a flat (N+1) int64 Fenwick Tree supporting 500,000+ updates/sec, O(log N) cumulative volume/range queries, and O(log N) P99 quantile lookup.
